items.title: Student-loan borrowers are taking on debt they can't pay off. There's a renewed push to prevent that.
items.summary: Sen. Elizabeth Warren is co-leading an effort to prevent student-loan borrowers from taking on unmanageable debt. Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Democratic lawmakers reintroduced legislation that would prevent unmanageable student debt burdens. It calls for strengthening accountability in the system that determines whether schools can receive federal aid. The Trump administration recently advanced its own proposal on college accreditation. Democratic lawmakers want to hold colleges accountable for unmanageable student-loan burdens . Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Dick Durbin are reintroducing the Accreditation Reform and Enhanced Accountability Act. It's aimed at strengthening accountability in the system that determines whether schools can receive federal aid for students. The bill would require the Department of Education to establish guidelines for evaluating colleges, including student-loan repayment outcomes and how much debt students take out postgrad compared to their earnings, according to a fact sheet on the legislation first viewed by Business Insider. The Biden administration found that, between 2021 and 2024, 1.7 million student-loan borrowers were defrauded by accredited schools, which lawmakers say bolsters the need for improved accreditation measures. The bill would also require accreditors to respond quickly to state and federal investigations regarding fraud or misconduct at schools and to increase transparency around accreditation decisions. "We need to overhaul our accreditation system to make sure students get an education that will improve their lives, not leave them jobless and buried in debt," Warren said in a statement. This legislation comes after the Education Department advanced its proposal to change the accreditation system, including by requiring accreditors to ensure that schools uphold free speech protections on campuses. It drew criticism from some negotiators who argued that First Amendment issues do not fall within an accreditor's purview. Undersecretary of Education Nicholas Kent said in a statement that the measures build on the department's goals of "lowering costs, simplifying repayment, connecting education to workforce needs, strengthening accountability, and restoring confidence in our accreditation system." Following staffing cuts at the Department of Education, lawmakers have been pushing for increased oversight over the student-loan repayment system. A recent report from the Office of the Inspector General found that some of the offices hardest hit by cuts were those that collected financial aid data on schools participating in federal student aid programs. items.title: What China's internet is saying about Moonshot's hot new Kimi model
items.summary: The Chinese internet has plenty to say about Moonshot AI's latest Kimi K3 model. China News Service/China News Service via Getty Images Moonshot AI's latest Kimi K3 model has China's internet abuzz. Weibo users weighed in on AI's computing demands, Elon Musk's reaction to Kimi K3, and the global AI race. "This race to build more powerful AI hardware isn't slowing down anytime soon," one user wrote. Moonshot AI's latest Kimi K3 model is giving China's internet plenty to talk about. The Chinese startup unveiled the open-weight model on Thursday, touting its ability to compete with leading systems from OpenAI and Anthropic at a fraction of the cost. Days later, Moonshot AI temporarily suspended new subscriptions , citing overwhelming demand that stretched its computing capacity. Like DeepSeek before it, Kimi K3 has become the latest Chinese AI model to spark discussion about China's emergence as a strong contender in the global AI race. On Weibo, China's version of X, posts about Kimi K3 surged to the top of the platform's trending list as users weighed in on the new model. Many saw it as another sign that Chinese AI companies can compete with the world's leading AI developers. At the same time, the launch of Kimi K3 also sparked a broader, spirited discussion about whether open-weight models could rival proprietary systems from US companies, and how China would meet the growing demand for computing power. Debates on compute One of the trending topics on the platform, titled "Kimi K3 sparks debate over AI compute," drew hundreds of users weighing in on what the model's launch means for the future of AI infrastructure. Moonshot AI says Kimi K3 converts computing power into AI capabilities more effectively than its predecessor. However, several popular posts on Weibo theorized that while more efficient models may lower the cost of individual tasks, they also drive wider adoption, which will drastically increase the overall demand for computing resources. "The competition is no longer about which single GPU is the most powerful. It's about how much computing capacity an entire cluster can handle," one user from Zhejiang wrote . "Put simply, the more capable AI becomes, the greater its appetite for computing power. This race to build more powerful AI hardware isn't slowing down anytime soon," another user from Shandong, a province south of Beijing, said . The Claude comparison Another Weibo trend, "Kimi K3 launch prompts online jabs at Anthropic," highlighted overseas reactions comparing Kimi K3 with Anthropic's Claude models. "Competition among AI software is likely to shift from focusing purely on performance to balancing both performance and token usage. In other words, it'll become a competition over value for money. It doesn't matter how powerful your model is if it uses too many tokens. And it doesn't matter how good it is if the monthly subscription is too expensive," one user from Jiangsu, a coastal province north of Shanghai, said . Beyond comparisons between the two models, others said that Kimi K3 also sparked a broader conversation about the global AI race. "They're starting to reflect on the system itself: Why didn't this kind of breakthrough happen in the US? Visas, the startup environment, and even internal management have all become topics of discussion," another user from Hubei, in central China, wrote . All about Elon The exchange between Moonshot AI and Elon Musk also dominated discussion on Weibo, where hashtags such as "Kimi responds to Musk's challenge," "Musk says new model could surpass Kimi," and "Kimi welcomes Musk" climbed the platform's trending list. On Saturday, Elon Musk said on X that initial training for xAI's next-generation Grok 4.6 model had entered its final stages, and that the 2 trillion-parameter model "might be able to exceed Kimi" while maintaining similar speed and token efficiency to Grok 4.5. In response, Moonshot AI's official Weibo account wrote , "Welcome to the 2 Trillion+ Club." Several popular posts described Moonshot AI's response as restrained and well handled. "It's great to see a Chinese team staying confident, letting its technology speak for itself in this global AI showdown," one user from Shaanxi wrote . "Calling it a 'club' broadened the conversation instead of turning it into a confrontation. This kind of healthy competition is refreshing and far better than trading insults," another user from Beijing wrote . "As Chinese and international AI companies keep challenging one another, the biggest beneficiaries will ultimately be the people who use these models," another user, also from Beijing, said . The Chinese internet has plenty to say about Moonshot AI's latest Kimi K3 model.

China News Service/China News Service via Getty Images

  • Moonshot AI's latest Kimi K3 model has China's internet abuzz.
  • Weibo users weighed in on AI's computing demands, Elon Musk's reaction to Kimi K3, and the global AI race.
  • "This race to build more powerful AI hardware isn't slowing down anytime soon," one user wrote.

Moonshot AI's latest Kimi K3 model is giving China's internet plenty to talk about.

The Chinese startup unveiled the open-weight model on Thursday, touting its ability to compete with leading systems from OpenAI and Anthropic at a fraction of the cost. Days later, Moonshot AI temporarily suspended new subscriptions, citing overwhelming demand that stretched its computing capacity.

Like DeepSeek before it, Kimi K3 has become the latest Chinese AI model to spark discussion about China's emergence as a strong contender in the global AI race.

On Weibo, China's version of X, posts about Kimi K3 surged to the top of the platform's trending list as users weighed in on the new model.

Many saw it as another sign that Chinese AI companies can compete with the world's leading AI developers.

At the same time, the launch of Kimi K3 also sparked a broader, spirited discussion about whether open-weight models could rival proprietary systems from US companies, and how China would meet the growing demand for computing power.

Debates on compute

One of the trending topics on the platform, titled "Kimi K3 sparks debate over AI compute," drew hundreds of users weighing in on what the model's launch means for the future of AI infrastructure.

Moonshot AI says Kimi K3 converts computing power into AI capabilities more effectively than its predecessor.

However, several popular posts on Weibo theorized that while more efficient models may lower the cost of individual tasks, they also drive wider adoption, which will drastically increase the overall demand for computing resources.

"The competition is no longer about which single GPU is the most powerful. It's about how much computing capacity an entire cluster can handle," one user from Zhejiang wrote.

"Put simply, the more capable AI becomes, the greater its appetite for computing power. This race to build more powerful AI hardware isn't slowing down anytime soon," another user from Shandong, a province south of Beijing, said.

The Claude comparison

Another Weibo trend, "Kimi K3 launch prompts online jabs at Anthropic," highlighted overseas reactions comparing Kimi K3 with Anthropic's Claude models.

"Competition among AI software is likely to shift from focusing purely on performance to balancing both performance and token usage. In other words, it'll become a competition over value for money. It doesn't matter how powerful your model is if it uses too many tokens. And it doesn't matter how good it is if the monthly subscription is too expensive," one user from Jiangsu, a coastal province north of Shanghai, said.

Beyond comparisons between the two models, others said that Kimi K3 also sparked a broader conversation about the global AI race.

"They're starting to reflect on the system itself: Why didn't this kind of breakthrough happen in the US? Visas, the startup environment, and even internal management have all become topics of discussion," another user from Hubei, in central China, wrote.

All about Elon

The exchange between Moonshot AI and Elon Musk also dominated discussion on Weibo, where hashtags such as "Kimi responds to Musk's challenge," "Musk says new model could surpass Kimi," and "Kimi welcomes Musk" climbed the platform's trending list.

On Saturday, Elon Musk said on X that initial training for xAI's next-generation Grok 4.6 model had entered its final stages, and that the 2 trillion-parameter model "might be able to exceed Kimi" while maintaining similar speed and token efficiency to Grok 4.5.

In response, Moonshot AI's official Weibo account wrote, "Welcome to the 2 Trillion+ Club."

Several popular posts described Moonshot AI's response as restrained and well handled.

"It's great to see a Chinese team staying confident, letting its technology speak for itself in this global AI showdown," one user from Shaanxi wrote.

"Calling it a 'club' broadened the conversation instead of turning it into a confrontation. This kind of healthy competition is refreshing and far better than trading insults," another user from Beijing wrote.

"As Chinese and international AI companies keep challenging one another, the biggest beneficiaries will ultimately be the people who use these models," another user, also from Beijing, said.

items.title: Curative CEO says company ditched a $600k-a-year Salesforce contract after vibecoding a CRM in 2 months
items.summary: Curative's CEO said maintaining the CRM is still a challenge. He still suggests it to other businesses. Frazer Harrison/Getty Images Curative's CEO said the company canceled an annual $600,000 Salesforce bill. His company replaced the CRM with a tool that AI helped build in two months. He's describing the SaaSpocalypse thesis: that AI coding tools will challenge software companies. Curative CEO and founder Fred Turner believes in the SaaSpocalypse . During an interview on the "20VC with Harry Stebbings" podcast, the health insurance executive was asked whether he bought the theory that software-as-a-service was dying. "Yes," Turner said, bluntly. When asked why, he said, "I see the number of contracts that we're canceling. We just recently canceled our Salesforce contract because we have an internal CRM that was vibecoded." That Salesforce contract cost Curative $600,000 a year, Turner said. He added that Curative built its replacement in two months. Overall, Curative plans to cut about 80% of its SaaS spending this year, according to Turner. The company is spending on AI instead, he said. He's describing the exact SaaSpocalypse fear that spooked Wall Street at the start of 2026. As AI coding agents quickly improved, investors feared that companies that bought software-as-a-service would turn to AI tools and build their own bespoke products. Software providers — such as Salesforce, Asana, DocuSign, ServiceNow, Adobe, and Workday — saw their stocks drop by 20% to 50% amid those snowballing concerns. Salesforce's CEO, Marc Benioff, has also strongly pushed back, saying that he's still seeing "incredible demand" for his products. He's also pointed out that Anthropic, the massive AI lab behind Claude, still uses Salesforce services. "If there is a 'SaaSpocalypse,' it may be eaten by the 'SaaS-quatch' because there are a lot of companies using a lot of SaaS because it just got better with agents," Benioff said during a February earnings call. A Salesforce spokesperson told Business Insider that 150,000 companies still use its platforms and highlighted that its tools are built to navigate complex healthcare patient regulations, such as HIPAA. "Our platform is built with trust and governance at its core," a Salesforce spokesperson told Business Insider. Turner acknowledged that replacing outside software with custom-built systems hasn't been perfect. Maintenance is "definitely one of the most challenging pieces," he said. He also said Curative's spending on Anthropic had surged as the company found more uses for AI. "Our Anthropic cost over the last six or seven months has 6x'd every month, from a base of a couple of tens of thousands of dollars, now up to millions of dollars a month," Turner said. "Eventually, we're going to have to stop that spending increase because it'll get unreasonable, but we just keep finding new things to do with it." For Curative, however, Turner said the economics would still work — even if Anthropic were to quintuple its prices . He pointed to Gwen, a bespoke AI agent Curative uses to negotiate contracts with doctors and other healthcare providers. Turner said completing one contract before AI had cost the company an average of $1,500 to $2,000. Gwen's average cost is about $70, he said. "What we've done is said, 'Well, now that we have the agent, we can do 10 times as many contracts this year as we could do last year,'" Turner said. "So, we're going to do 10 times, and then we're going to try and do 20 times, and we would just do a lot more volume than you could possibly have done with a human team." Curative didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Salesforce declined to provide a comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I'm a product manager who grew my salary from $40K to over $250K. Getting an MBA changed the game for me.
items.summary: Courtesy of Kris Martin; BI Kent Shen is a 37-year-old product manager in Seattle. Business Insider has verified Shen's income and employment history with documentation. The following as-told-to essay has been edited for length and clarity. I came from a lower-income family in Canada, and after graduating from the University of Waterloo in 2012, I spent a few years trying to build a business that ultimately failed. When I returned to the workforce, I felt two years behind many of the applicants I was competing against. Now, I'm a product manager at Expedia making over $250,000 a year. It took until last year for me to shake off imposter syndrome . After a decade of setbacks, I finally feel comfortable in my role and confident that I belong there. I am thriving now and feel capable of continuing to grow and earn more. Here's my salary journey. Operations analyst, $40,000 CAD → $45,000 CAD I was hired at TD Securities in 2014 on a six-month contract at $40,000 CAD annually. In 2015, I was hired full-time as an operations analyst at a base salary of $45,000 CAD. Previously, I hadn't thought I'd be a strong candidate for a top MBA program , due to my low undergraduate GPA. While working here, though, I met a coworker who helped me see that a top MBA program allows for career switching and pivoting. Salary Journeys is Business Insider's first-person series following real people and their real paychecks — how they built their income, what it means for their lives, and what they learned along the way. If you're willing to share how your salary has changed over time, please fill out this Google Form . Manager, $68,000 CAD In 2017, I joined RBC Capital Markets as a manager, earning $68,000 CAD. I took the GMAT multiple times before reaching a score I felt comfortable applying to business school with in 2018. The University of Michigan's Stephen M. Ross School of Business was my top choice, but I was in the bottom 10% of applicant profiles. The standard strategy is to apply for schools in multiple tiers: reach schools, target schools, and safety schools. Michigan, along with MIT, was one of my reach schools, while UCLA was my target school. I picked my reach schools because of my sports writing experience; after graduating from undergrad, I'd written and edited for a fantasy basketball website. Michigan has a heavy sports culture , while MIT Sloan hosts the Sloan Sports Analytics Conference every year. I used that experience, along with a strong recommendation from the site's owner, to shape an application story aligned with the sports culture. I was rejected by UCLA, but Michigan took a chance on me, giving me the opportunity to pursue my MBA. Business school student, $0 I moved to the US for business school. It was a pretty big transition and the farthest from home I'd ever lived. I took on debt to attend, but it was worth it for the opportunity to pivot into an industry I desired and to increase my earning opportunity. The salary increase I later got ended up more than paying off the debt. Halfway through my first year at Michigan in 2019, the pandemic hit, making the transition to the US even more difficult than usual. The in-person recruiting and networking that had drawn me to the program suddenly moved to Zoom. COVID also limited the internship opportunities available, and I was rejected from consulting internships. I accepted an internship at a small tech startup in corporate strategy, which gave me valuable business experience. I built relationships within the company and halfway through, I shifted from corporate strategy to product management. Product Strategy Manager, $195,000, plus signing bonus I struggled to find a job after graduating with an MBA in 2021. It was terrible; I had to take on a job I hated for a bit, and left that job within four months. At the time, it didn't feel good, but I knew I just needed to wait out the bad COVID job market. Pivoting into tech is extremely difficult for those not coming from tech and engineering backgrounds. There is zero chance I'd be where I am without doing an MBA at Michigan. As the tech market began to heat up, I leveraged my startup internship and finance background to pivot into tech and secure a product strategy role at Expedia in January 2022, focused on insurance. I was paid a base salary of $165,000 and around $30,000 in restricted stock units, plus a $33,000 signing bonus. Product Manager, $250,000 I got progressive raises over the years. Last year, I was given a broad strategic mandate and full ownership over the work. The products I launched performed strongly, and that experience significantly strengthened my confidence. This came with a $14,000 salary bump, plus some RSUs, bringing my total compensation to over $250,000. I'm gunning for promotion this year. For a long time, I had an "I'm just happy to be here" mindset. In my 20s, while friends were buying homes, I was saving aggressively and investing in my future so I could afford business school. I spent years feeling like one setback could put me in financial trouble. Over the past few years, that has changed. I've been able to focus less on simply staying afloat and more on career development, growth, and the value I can create. I feel well compensated now, but I also believe the impact I can have in the future will be worth even more. My wife and I have a long-term goal of building a net worth of around $3 million Even in this higher income bracket, I'm still extremely frugal . My wife, who works in education, is the same way. Even as our incomes have grown, we've kept our spending in check. We budget aggressively , invest carefully, and take calculated risks. I think I would remain frugal even if my salary tripled. We are planning for the next 10 to 20 years. We save and invest roughly $100,000 to $250,000 annually while still making room for things we value, including budgeting for travel. I don't have a specific salary goal in mind; net worth in the long run is a function of salary, spending habits, and investment habits. As our salaries grow, we hope to save and invest even more. Our long-term goal is to build an inflation-adjusted net worth of about $3 million, enough to give us real security if either of us were laid off and make us less dependent on the job market. If you're interested in sharing your salary journey, please fill out this Google Form . Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Courtesy of Kris Martin; BI

Kent Shen is a 37-year-old product manager in Seattle. Business Insider has verified Shen's income and employment history with documentation. The following as-told-to essay has been edited for length and clarity.

I came from a lower-income family in Canada, and after graduating from the University of Waterloo in 2012, I spent a few years trying to build a business that ultimately failed.

When I returned to the workforce, I felt two years behind many of the applicants I was competing against.

Now, I'm a product manager at Expedia making over $250,000 a year.

It took until last year for me to shake off imposter syndrome. After a decade of setbacks, I finally feel comfortable in my role and confident that I belong there. I am thriving now and feel capable of continuing to grow and earn more.

Here's my salary journey.

Operations analyst, $40,000 CAD → $45,000 CAD

I was hired at TD Securities in 2014 on a six-month contract at $40,000 CAD annually. In 2015, I was hired full-time as an operations analyst at a base salary of $45,000 CAD.

Previously, I hadn't thought I'd be a strong candidate for a top MBA program, due to my low undergraduate GPA. While working here, though, I met a coworker who helped me see that a top MBA program allows for career switching and pivoting.

Salary Journeys is Business Insider's first-person series following real people and their real paychecks — how they built their income, what it means for their lives, and what they learned along the way. If you're willing to share how your salary has changed over time, please fill out this Google Form.

Manager, $68,000 CAD

In 2017, I joined RBC Capital Markets as a manager, earning $68,000 CAD.

I took the GMAT multiple times before reaching a score I felt comfortable applying to business school with in 2018.

The University of Michigan's Stephen M. Ross School of Business was my top choice, but I was in the bottom 10% of applicant profiles. The standard strategy is to apply for schools in multiple tiers: reach schools, target schools, and safety schools.

Michigan, along with MIT, was one of my reach schools, while UCLA was my target school. I picked my reach schools because of my sports writing experience; after graduating from undergrad, I'd written and edited for a fantasy basketball website. Michigan has a heavy sports culture, while MIT Sloan hosts the Sloan Sports Analytics Conference every year.

I used that experience, along with a strong recommendation from the site's owner, to shape an application story aligned with the sports culture.

I was rejected by UCLA, but Michigan took a chance on me, giving me the opportunity to pursue my MBA.

Business school student, $0

I moved to the US for business school. It was a pretty big transition and the farthest from home I'd ever lived.

I took on debt to attend, but it was worth it for the opportunity to pivot into an industry I desired and to increase my earning opportunity. The salary increase I later got ended up more than paying off the debt.

Halfway through my first year at Michigan in 2019, the pandemic hit, making the transition to the US even more difficult than usual. The in-person recruiting and networking that had drawn me to the program suddenly moved to Zoom. COVID also limited the internship opportunities available, and I was rejected from consulting internships.

I accepted an internship at a small tech startup in corporate strategy, which gave me valuable business experience. I built relationships within the company and halfway through, I shifted from corporate strategy to product management.

Product Strategy Manager, $195,000, plus signing bonus

I struggled to find a job after graduating with an MBA in 2021. It was terrible; I had to take on a job I hated for a bit, and left that job within four months. At the time, it didn't feel good, but I knew I just needed to wait out the bad COVID job market.

Pivoting into tech is extremely difficult for those not coming from tech and engineering backgrounds. There is zero chance I'd be where I am without doing an MBA at Michigan.

As the tech market began to heat up, I leveraged my startup internship and finance background to pivot into tech and secure a product strategy role at Expedia in January 2022, focused on insurance. I was paid a base salary of $165,000 and around $30,000 in restricted stock units, plus a $33,000 signing bonus.

Product Manager, $250,000

I got progressive raises over the years. Last year, I was given a broad strategic mandate and full ownership over the work. The products I launched performed strongly, and that experience significantly strengthened my confidence.

This came with a $14,000 salary bump, plus some RSUs, bringing my total compensation to over $250,000.

I'm gunning for promotion this year.

For a long time, I had an "I'm just happy to be here" mindset. In my 20s, while friends were buying homes, I was saving aggressively and investing in my future so I could afford business school. I spent years feeling like one setback could put me in financial trouble.

Over the past few years, that has changed. I've been able to focus less on simply staying afloat and more on career development, growth, and the value I can create.

I feel well compensated now, but I also believe the impact I can have in the future will be worth even more.

My wife and I have a long-term goal of building a net worth of around $3 million

Even in this higher income bracket, I'm still extremely frugal.

My wife, who works in education, is the same way. Even as our incomes have grown, we've kept our spending in check. We budget aggressively, invest carefully, and take calculated risks. I think I would remain frugal even if my salary tripled.

We are planning for the next 10 to 20 years. We save and invest roughly $100,000 to $250,000 annually while still making room for things we value, including budgeting for travel.

I don't have a specific salary goal in mind; net worth in the long run is a function of salary, spending habits, and investment habits. As our salaries grow, we hope to save and invest even more.

Our long-term goal is to build an inflation-adjusted net worth of about $3 million, enough to give us real security if either of us were laid off and make us less dependent on the job market.

If you're interested in sharing your salary journey, please fill out this Google Form.

items.title: OpenAI faces stark doubts about ChatGPT ads. It's beginning the long fight to prove them wrong.
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Brendan Smialowski  / AFP via Getty Images OpenAI has lofty goals for ChatGPT's ads business, an attempt to monetize the blockbuster app. The product is still rudimentary, advertisers said, though it's changing every week. OpenAI's ad revenue projections aren't logical, one analyst told Business Insider. OpenAI badly wants a piece of the advertising empires that Google and Meta built, and it has a lot of catch-up to do. The AI startup began selling ads on its blockbuster ChatGPT product in February, and the ensuing months have brought geographic expansions, added capabilities, and new advertisers onto the platform. Still, ChatGPT's ads business has a long way to go before it rakes in anything like the revenue OpenAI has projected, and customers using ChatGPT for advertising told Business Insider that the product is still rudimentary. Advertising is becoming a major opportunity for OpenAI. ChatGPT now has around 1 billion monthly users. If OpenAI can grow into a Google- or Meta-sized ad seller, it could rake in billions of dollars and can rely less on business deals than its rival Anthropic does. That will require a long, hard push — and overcoming stark doubts. OpenAI said in March that its ad business had hit $100 million in annual recurring revenue. In April, the Information and Axios reported that OpenAI was forecasting about $2.4 billion in ads revenue in 2026 and around $100 billion in 2030. "I don't think there's any chance they hit that goal," said Nate Elliott, an analyst at the data firm EMARKETER. To hit those numbers, OpenAI would need to dramatically grow its user count, handily beat Google in the consumer AI market, price its ads aggressively, and fill ChatGPT with an "unbearably" high load of ads, Elliott told Business Insider, describing his firm's analysis. "We look at their numbers and the assumptions required to get there, and we don't see any of those assumptions as logical or reasonable," Elliott said of OpenAI's projections. EMARKETER predicts that the entire chatbot ads market will make less than $1 billion this year. In comparison, Google generated over $294 billion in ads revenue in 2025. While advertisers are excited about OpenAI's offering, they said they are still adjusting to the relative lack of tools for campaign creation, measurement, and reporting. Google and Meta's advertising tools offer more features for metrics, testing, and videos. An OpenAI spokesperson told Business Insider the company is still learning from advertisers and expanding the platform's capabilities, though they did not respond to the EMARKETER analysis. They added that ChatGPT's ads are still in their early days and are only appearing in seven countries so far. OpenAI is careful not to pump too many ads into ChatGPT Initially, OpenAI kept ChatGPT ad-free. CEO Sam Altman called the combination of AI and ads a "last resort" in 2024. The company's financial concerns won out, and under its former applications CEO, Fidji Simo , it began holding discussions about what forms ads could take. A pilot round of advertising began in February, with major companies committing hundreds of thousands of dollars. Business Insider asked OpenAI's ads chief, Dave Dugan , at Cannes about early advertisers not being able to buy as many ads as they wanted, and he said that the company "started very conservatively at the beginning to focus on the user experience." In May, OpenAI launched a tool that let other companies create and manage their own ads. The tool is simple, without many of the bells and whistles that Google and Meta have added over the years to their advertising products. It wasn't until July that marketers could target ChatGPT ads to a geographic area within the US, rather than the entire country. When marketing startup Launch10 tested ChatGPT's advertising tool, its campaign got a far lower click-through rate than on Google ads, said CEO Greg Hockenbrocht. He added that he thought the tool would have more features for generating ad copy and testing variants. "My own expectation was that given it was an ads platform launched by one of the leading foundation model companies, that the platform would be a little bit more, call it, 'AI-native,'" Hockenbrocht told Business Insider. Still, Hockenbrocht sees the new addition of location targeting as proof of improvement. And during a recent monthlong ad campaign, Hockenbrocht said that impressions and clicks increased noticeably over time. "I give credit to the OpenAI team," he said. "They're shipping quickly, which is good. I think they're going to have to continue to do that." Advertisers have to adjust their expectations Unlike Google's keyword bidding or Meta's audience targeting, ChatGPT ads pop up based on a multi-step conversation. The new format is great for some advertisers. AI text-to-speech startup Speechify has been advertising with OpenAI since the early pilots. Its chief business officer, Rohan Pavuluri, told Business Insider that because developers ask ChatGPT for advice and Speechify ads appear under text-to-speech tool comparisons, the startup has seen a stream of new business. Kevin Roy, the CEO of advertising agency GreenBanana SEO, told Business Insider that while his firm's clients have been excited about the prospect of reaching ChatGPT's broad audience , they need to rethink their ads to focus on the questions a user might provide in their ChatGPT prompt. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

  • OpenAI has lofty goals for ChatGPT's ads business, an attempt to monetize the blockbuster app.
  • The product is still rudimentary, advertisers said, though it's changing every week.
  • OpenAI's ad revenue projections aren't logical, one analyst told Business Insider.

OpenAI badly wants a piece of the advertising empires that Google and Meta built, and it has a lot of catch-up to do.

The AI startup began selling ads on its blockbuster ChatGPT product in February, and the ensuing months have brought geographic expansions, added capabilities, and new advertisers onto the platform. Still, ChatGPT's ads business has a long way to go before it rakes in anything like the revenue OpenAI has projected, and customers using ChatGPT for advertising told Business Insider that the product is still rudimentary.

Advertising is becoming a major opportunity for OpenAI. ChatGPT now has around 1 billion monthly users. If OpenAI can grow into a Google- or Meta-sized ad seller, it could rake in billions of dollars and can rely less on business deals than its rival Anthropic does. That will require a long, hard push — and overcoming stark doubts.

OpenAI said in March that its ad business had hit $100 million in annual recurring revenue. In April, the Information and Axios reported that OpenAI was forecasting about $2.4 billion in ads revenue in 2026 and around $100 billion in 2030.

"I don't think there's any chance they hit that goal," said Nate Elliott, an analyst at the data firm EMARKETER.

To hit those numbers, OpenAI would need to dramatically grow its user count, handily beat Google in the consumer AI market, price its ads aggressively, and fill ChatGPT with an "unbearably" high load of ads, Elliott told Business Insider, describing his firm's analysis.

"We look at their numbers and the assumptions required to get there, and we don't see any of those assumptions as logical or reasonable," Elliott said of OpenAI's projections.

EMARKETER predicts that the entire chatbot ads market will make less than $1 billion this year. In comparison, Google generated over $294 billion in ads revenue in 2025.

While advertisers are excited about OpenAI's offering, they said they are still adjusting to the relative lack of tools for campaign creation, measurement, and reporting. Google and Meta's advertising tools offer more features for metrics, testing, and videos.

An OpenAI spokesperson told Business Insider the company is still learning from advertisers and expanding the platform's capabilities, though they did not respond to the EMARKETER analysis. They added that ChatGPT's ads are still in their early days and are only appearing in seven countries so far.

OpenAI is careful not to pump too many ads into ChatGPT

Initially, OpenAI kept ChatGPT ad-free. CEO Sam Altman called the combination of AI and ads a "last resort" in 2024. The company's financial concerns won out, and under its former applications CEO, Fidji Simo, it began holding discussions about what forms ads could take.

A pilot round of advertising began in February, with major companies committing hundreds of thousands of dollars. Business Insider asked OpenAI's ads chief, Dave Dugan, at Cannes about early advertisers not being able to buy as many ads as they wanted, and he said that the company "started very conservatively at the beginning to focus on the user experience."

In May, OpenAI launched a tool that let other companies create and manage their own ads. The tool is simple, without many of the bells and whistles that Google and Meta have added over the years to their advertising products. It wasn't until July that marketers could target ChatGPT ads to a geographic area within the US, rather than the entire country.

When marketing startup Launch10 tested ChatGPT's advertising tool, its campaign got a far lower click-through rate than on Google ads, said CEO Greg Hockenbrocht. He added that he thought the tool would have more features for generating ad copy and testing variants.

"My own expectation was that given it was an ads platform launched by one of the leading foundation model companies, that the platform would be a little bit more, call it, 'AI-native,'" Hockenbrocht told Business Insider.

Still, Hockenbrocht sees the new addition of location targeting as proof of improvement. And during a recent monthlong ad campaign, Hockenbrocht said that impressions and clicks increased noticeably over time.

"I give credit to the OpenAI team," he said. "They're shipping quickly, which is good. I think they're going to have to continue to do that."

Advertisers have to adjust their expectations

Unlike Google's keyword bidding or Meta's audience targeting, ChatGPT ads pop up based on a multi-step conversation.

The new format is great for some advertisers. AI text-to-speech startup Speechify has been advertising with OpenAI since the early pilots. Its chief business officer, Rohan Pavuluri, told Business Insider that because developers ask ChatGPT for advice and Speechify ads appear under text-to-speech tool comparisons, the startup has seen a stream of new business.

Kevin Roy, the CEO of advertising agency GreenBanana SEO, told Business Insider that while his firm's clients have been excited about the prospect of reaching ChatGPT's broad audience, they need to rethink their ads to focus on the questions a user might provide in their ChatGPT prompt. They also need to be OK with seeing less data about their ads, for now.

"There's very few levers that we can pull in Chat ads, compared to the dozens and dozens of levers in Google Ads," Roy said.

Dugan pitched OpenAI's speed and AI usage as a way to catch up in advertising when he talked to Business Insider in June.

"Our engineers use our own products like Codex to build out the product set, and that's meant that the pace of our launches, often on a weekly basis, is much faster than anything I've experienced before," Dugan said.

Since launching its ad product, OpenAI has added digital ad standbys such as cost-per-click bidding and conversion-tracking tools.

items.title: The Proliferation of Deepfakes Is Profoundly Changing the Way Teenagers Use the Internet
items.summary: AI-generated sexual content is rapidly remaking young people’s lives as they confront sex and dating — and the effects are as sweeping as they are poorly understood. That’s according to a new survey from the nonprofit Common Sense Media, in which researchers dug into how youth are interacting with these new technologies. What they found suggests that the proliferation of this kind of content — and the harm it’s already causing — demand urgent attention. The nationally representative survey drew on insights from 1,314 teenagers aged 13 to 17, as well as additional data from interviews and focus groups, and defines AI-generated sexual content as deepfaked nude images or pornographic material of real people, AI images and videos of people depicted in revealing or sexually explicit scenarios, or “any other sexual content made by AI.” It comes as middle and high schools around the country grapple with an explosion of nonconsensual deepfakes of minors that have largely been created and disseminated by their peers. “For a good chunk of teens, one, they’re being exposed to this content — but two, they are creating and sharing this content,” Supreet Mann, Common Sense Media’s director of research and the lead author of the report, told Futurism . “And when they’re doing that, it’s very often of people they know personally or themselves.” The report found that nearly half of high school and middle school-aged teens have seen what they believed to be AI-generated sexual content, with most reporting that they discovered it accidentally, often by way of social media. Of the teens who reported seeing this kind of content, about 64 percent said it depicted recognizable celebrities, while 24 percent shared that the content showed either them or someone they knew in real life. Roughly eight percent of teens, meanwhile, reported creating deepfakes or other AI-generated sexual content themselves, while another 13 percent shared that they knew someone who had generated sexual content using AI. Of that cohort, more than 60 percent noted that the “content depicted themselves or people they know personally, like peers, friends, or current and former romantic partners.” The anxiety around this kind of material has driven some kids to change their behaviors online, the report found. Around 67 percent of surveyed teens shared that they were at least somewhat worried that they could be impacted by deepfakes, and nearly 40 percent have made their social media accounts private, are limiting what they share, or have fully deleted social media. “About two-thirds of teens indicated that they were worried about this, and many of those young people are changing their online behaviors because of that fear… that’s a very interesting tell of how young people are thinking about the content, and they’re thinking about this lack of agency that they have in the space,” said Mann. And while it’s not a bad thing for kids to think critically about their online presence, Mann added, as it stands, the burden is falling heavily on the shoulders of teens themselves to cope with the deepfake influx. “Why are young people being forced to police themselves,” asked the researcher, “when this really shouldn’t be their burden to carry?” It’s easy to see why teens are so frightened. With a photo and a click of a few buttons, easily-accessible “ nudify ” apps, which are widely available online and through app stores , have made it trivially easy to artificially undress people without their consent. General-use chatbots — most notably xAI’s Grok — have also been used to create deepfakes, including of minors. Deepfake scandals have rocked towns across the US, primarily impacting girls , who have described experiencing crushing anxiety and panic attacks, suicidal thoughts, and a deep loss of trust in their peers and social world as a result of the disturbing content. Some of the teenage creators of deepfake porn, some of whom have confessed to generating hundreds of the images, have been arrested and criminally charged. (AI-generated sexual imagery depicting minors is considered to be illegal child sexual abuse material under federal law.) One family in Louisiana sued a school district after their 13-year-old daughter — after first attempting to alert school officials — was expelled for physically confronting a classmate who had created and shared nonconsensual deepfakes of her and her friends. The boy who generated the images received no discipline, the lawsuit alleged. One bright spot from the survey, Mann noted, was that many kids shared that they want to speak with trusted adults in their lives about this strange new world, but aren’t quite sure how to. “Only one in five [teens] said that they had ever talked to a trusted adult about this. But a third of teens said that they want to talk to someone, they just don’t know how to have the conversation,” said Mann. Younger teens, she added, are more likely to want to talk with trusted adults about this kind of material than older kids are — while one in ten teens shared that they would be most comfortable talking to a chatbot about what they were seeing. To Mann, those responses signal that “kids are open to having these conversations,” and that “getting in there early and creating that space for conversation is really key.” There’s a “unique window of opportunity for parents to start having these conversations with their kiddos, and to just not wait on the conversation,” Mann added. “We we don’t want our kids to be turning to AI chatbots to have conversations, or to not have these conversations at all.” In addition to parents, schools, policymakers, and tech companies — the latter of which are building the tools being used to generate this material, and run platforms where young people are encountering AI-generated sexual content — need to be proactive about understanding this kind of material and mitigating its harms. One challenge is to limit the creation of deepfakes to begin with, an effort that has some local officials looking at app stores as a possible chokepoint in the deepfake supply chain: last week, the city of San Francisco commanded Apple and Google to remove “nudify” apps from their respective app stores. “This is really a this is something that needs to be tackled from all angles,” said Mann. In the meantime, it’s kids who are confronting the lived impact of artificial porn and deepfakes in their personal and social lives. “We grew as AI grew. We grew up together. Adults don’t have the same life experience that we do,” one 17-year-old girl told researchers. “They don’t understand how advanced and how intense AI is.” More on deepfakes: Elon Musk’s xAI, Which is Being Sued Over AI-Generated Sexual Deepfakes, Sues Grok User Over AI-Generated Sexual Deepfakes The post The Proliferation of Deepfakes Is Profoundly Changing the Way Teenagers Use the Internet appeared first on Futurism .

The Rundown: The U.S. government is exploring ways to restrict Chinese AI models, according to a new Axios report, with Moonshot’s near-frontier Kimi K3 release reviving a push that was previously struck down by internal anti-regulation efforts.

The details:

  • Officials weighed liability rules for companies hosting Chinese models, a public security warning, and cutting off labs through a trade blacklist.

  • Previous plans had been struck down, but Axios said the departure of "key voices" has left "national security hawks" gaining ground at the White House.

  • Politico's Sophia Cai countered the Axios reporting, saying that Commerce "is NOT moving forward on banning Chinese models at this time."

  • Before the report, former AI czar David Sacks wrote that the "leading closed labs" want "the government to eliminate their open-source competition."

Why it matters: New OAI employee Dean Ball ignited X with his thoughts on K3, but his prediction quickly looks validated if Axios’ reporting holds. With China's advances and thin homegrown open options, U.S. companies get stuck in the middle in the event of a ban — pushed off the cheapest capable models with no replacement.

AI TRAINING⚓️ Make AI note-taking easier with a “Captain’s Log”

The Rundown: In this guide, you will learn how to stop losing ideas and follow-ups by building an AI “Captain’s Log.” Capture quick Granola notes, then use ChatGPT to turn them into a daily summary and task list automatically.

Step-by-step:

  1. Install Granola on your iPhone and PC. Then, go to iPhone Settings → Action Button → Shortcut → Granola → New Note. Holding it starts a voice note

  2. In ChatGPT, connect Granola. Create a ‘Captain’s Log’ project and tell it to organize periodic Granola notes by day, summarize them, and track open tasks

  3. Record short logs after meetings, or whenever an idea hits, starting with “Captain’s Log”. Granola auto-creates enhanced notes and keeps transcripts

  4. Tell ChatGPT to read latest notes, create an end-of-day summary, update a running task list, and turn the process into a skill that runs daily at 7 p.m.

Pro tip: Use ChatGPT mode, not Codex. If it tries to control your browser instead of reading your notes, type @Granola and select the plugin directly.

Get resources, prompts, and full step-by-step video guide here.

The Rundown: Engineering leaders can't afford to keep making AI investment decisions on intuition. Datadog's free AI Playbook gives you a practical framework to move from ad-hoc AI bets to evidence-driven systems.

In the ebook, you'll get:

  • Three enabling capabilities that make AI wins repeatable across teams

  • Ways to keep humans in the loop as AI agents take on more work

  • A 90-day action checklist

Get the ebook.

OPENAI🔒 OpenAI’s math star model tries to break containment

Image source: Images 2.0 / The Rundown

The Rundown: OpenAI published a blog revealing that it benched its unreleased model behind May's Erdős breakthrough after the system kept finding holes in its sandbox, and restored access once new safeguards to track work sessions were ready.

The details:

  • OpenAI built the unnamed system for longer jobs that outlast a normal chat, and used it in May to help settle an 80-year-old Erdős geometry problem.

  • In one test, a scanner caught the model hunting other systems’ private answers, admitting that it tried to slip them through in scrambled pieces.

  • In another, the system searched for roughly 60 minutes until it beat an internet block, then put its confidential findings on GitHub against orders.

  • OpenAI said the misaligned behaviors caused the company to pause internal deployment to improve its monitoring, safeguards, and visibility.

Why it matters: Models are starting to be able to work autonomously for longer and longer sessions, making both monitoring and keeping super-capable systems in check an increasingly difficult but important problem. These systems admitted and announced their objectives, but the next batch might be less forthcoming.

items.title: Lettuce lovers are confused and afraid
items.summary: Salad fans told Business Insider how they were faring as Cyclospora spreads. Jaylin Eaves; Austin Kreitler; Diana Umana The spread of Cyclospora has some eaters cutting down on fresh lettuce. Five salad lovers told Business Insider about their strategies, from avoiding iceberg to cutting fresh produce entirely. "I can't keep track of what I can't eat anymore," one lettuce lover said. "I'm hungry!" Baldwin Williams Jr. wanted lunch. He was craving Jersey Mike's, but then remembered that his sub would have shredded lettuce. Then he thought about Qdoba — but remembered his bowl would have lettuce, too. Sure, the 28-year-old from Maryland could've gotten his meal without the leafy greens. But Williams firmly believes that "the lettuce is the base." Williams has tried to avoid lettuce ever since news broke about Cyclospora, a microscopic parasite that causes the intestinal illness cyclosporiasis. While the exact culprit isn't clear, lettuce — and specifically iceberg — has been a focus for the Food and Drug Administration. There's also been some back-and-forth surrounding Taylor Farms' link to the spread. While some ignore the warnings , others are waving goodbye to their greens. That's especially upsetting for salad heads, craving a crisp summer bowl to beat the heat. "It's frustrating, confusing, and annoying," Williams said. Baldwin Williams Jr. loves lettuce in his salads and sandwiches. "Vegetables are important," he said. Baldwin Williams Jr. The big salad confusion Austin Kreitler loves salad so much that he's dedicated a whole Instagram page to it. The 29-year-old from Phoenix said he has had a salad with his dinner almost every night since he was young. Kreitler especially misses the salad bars he used to frequent for lunch, many of which shut down during the pandemic. Now, he rates all of his Caesar salads online. Kreitler was relieved that iceberg lettuce was the focus (notably not a common ingredient in a Caesar). "I still want to eat them, because they're one of my favorite meals," Kreitler said of salads. Still, Kreitler has kept up with the "scary" news and cut bagged lettuce out of his diet. He watches local news in the evening, scrolls social media, and reads online articles. He's found it hard to keep up. "It's definitely confusing," he said. "One day it's this, and another day it's not." That was a common sentiment among the lettuce lovers I spoke to. Jaylin Eaves, a 29-year-old comedian based in Rhode Island, has a salad twice a week. "I like the crunch," she said. After hearing about the outbreak, Eaves said that she's been leaning on other foods. She called the switch-up "devastating," turning a food she believed was healthy into a source of worry. Eaves did fold once. At a recent catered event, someone made her a plate that included a Caesar salad . She started eating it before remembering about the outbreak. "I don't think it serves me to be paranoid," she said, referring to it as a "little oopsie." "I feel like every morning we find out new food groups we can't eat," she said. "I can't keep track of what I can't eat anymore. I'm going to starve, and I'm hungry!" Missing our slop bowls Mandy Enright isn't confused — but she is concerned. As a dietitian, the 45-year-old from Asbury Park has followed the news closely. She purchases her lettuce from local farm markets, so she feels safe eating it. Enright said that it was especially rough in summer, a time when people want to eat fresh, cold foods rather than "slaving over hot stoves in our kitchens." It's also difficult when she eats out. Enright recently eyed a nice salad on a restaurant menu, before second-guessing herself. She chose a cooked vegetable instead. Dietician Mandy Enright purchases her lettuce at farm markets. Mandy Enright For many, ordering salads is a knee-jerk reaction. They're on many menus, and can be a reliable source of nutrients. That's especially true for office workers, for whom a midday "slop bowl" has become the norm. After the Cyclospora outbreak, some eaters are putting more thought into their meals. Diana Umana called herself a "salad girlie." The 28-year-old from New York said she ate lettuce every day, frequenting a Bronx restaurant for her chicken Caesar salad hit. Then Umana heard the news and cut lettuce from her diet. She's been cooking her vegetables, something she said has led to too many carb-heavy meals. "I'm someone who's a meal-prepper, so I'm used to having the same thing every day," Umana said. "What do you mean I have to think? I hate that for me." There's a good reason to think, after all. While there haven't been any reported deaths from cyclosporiasis, the illness is certainly unpleasant . "When I hear the phrase 'explosive diarrhea' being used," Williams said, "it's like… no. Whole lot of no." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: OnePlus to Exit US and Europe as Oppo Restructures, With Full Shutdown in China and India Expected by 2027
items.summary: Oppo is reorganizing its smartphone division, reportedly ending sales and operations for OnePlus in the United States and Europe as soon as this week, according to a Bloomberg report cited by BetaNews. The report also states that OnePlus plans to wind down in China and India by 2027, marking the end of the brand that launched in 2013 with competitively priced Android flagships. Additionally, Realme, another brand owned by Oppo, will exit the Chinese market. The restructuring is linked to ongoing challenges caused by the global memory shortage, which has increased component costs across the smartphone industry. Oppo’s Plan to Wind Down OnePlus and Realme Bloomberg reports that OnePlus plans to start shutting down operations in the US and Europe within a few days, according to a person familiar with the matter who requested anonymity due to the private nature of the plan. This move is part of a broader restructuring at the parent company Oppo, officially known as Guangdong Oppo Mobile Telecommunications Corporation Ltd. BetaNews states that no new OnePlus devices will be released in the US or European markets after the company's exit. The timeline for the wider shutdown in China and India has not been publicly confirmed by Oppo, and Bloomberg suggests that more details are likely to be announced in the coming weeks and months. The restructuring also impacts Realme. Bloomberg reports that Realme will soon exit the Chinese market and shift its device sales focus to Nordic countries. Oppo will now prioritize its main market presence in Central Europe. This three-brand restructuring will significantly reduce Oppo's global footprint. Before the changes, OnePlus, Realme, and Oppo sold products in overlapping regions, with OnePlus targeting performance enthusiasts, Realme focusing on entry-level and mid-range devices, and Oppo serving mainstream consumers. Memory Shortage Fallout and What OnePlus Owners Should Do Oppo is the latest smartphone manufacturer to publicly cite a memory shortage as a factor in a major business decision. Prices for DRAM and NAND memory chips have increased through 2025 and into 2026, squeezing margins on lower-priced Android devices where component costs account for a larger part of the retail price. BetaNews notes that the immediate impact of the shortage is being felt first in the US and European OnePlus markets. Oppo has not released a detailed statement outlining the full timeline, affected product lines, or how existing device warranties and software support will be managed in markets where OnePlus is exiting. For users currently using OnePlus devices in the US or Europe, it is advisable to take a few practical steps while the transition unfolds, based on the information available so far: Check the warranty status of each device and note the purchase date and retailer, as warranty claim processes may change as regional operations wind down. Save copies of driver files, unlock tools, and firmware images related to your specific model, since download servers linked to regional stores could be affected by the restructuring. Back up your device data locally and to a cloud service not tied to your OnePlus account, in case support services are consolidated or migrated to Oppo infrastructure. Avoid making major accessory purchases for unreleased OnePlus devices in these regions, as no new product launches are expected there. Keep an eye on Oppo's official announcements for updates on ongoing software and security support for existing OnePlus phones in the affected areas. Oppo has not confirmed whether existing OnePlus devices in the US and Europe will continue to receive Android updates and security patches on schedule or if support periods will be shortened as part of the restructuring. Unanswered Questions About Oppo’s Restructuring and OnePlus’s Future Bloomberg's source suggests that the exit from the US and Europe could start as early as this week. While reports indicate that OnePlus might shut down in China and India by 2027, Oppo has not officially confirmed this, and no formal statement has been issued regarding the sequence of market exits, staff impact, or the future of the OnePlus brand following the restructuring. Similarly, reports based on Bloomberg's information indicate that Realme is leaving the Chinese market and refocusing on the Nordic region, but Oppo has not officially announced these plans. More details are expected in the coming weeks as Oppo continues to formalize its restructuring. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post OnePlus to Exit US and Europe as Oppo Restructures, With Full Shutdown in China and India Expected by 2027 appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: Book Writers Sue Google Over Alleged Use of Copyrighted Books to Train Gemini
items.summary: Hachette Book Group, Cengage Learning, Elsevier, author Scott Turow, and S.C.R.I.B.E., Inc. have filed a proposed federal class-action lawsuit against Google . They accuse the company of copying copyrighted books and journal articles without permission to train its Gemini AI models. The lawsuit was filed on July 10, 2026. The case, Hachette Book Group Inc. et al. v. Google LLC, is under case number 1:26-cv-05870 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. The complaint describes Google's alleged actions as "one of the most prolific infringements of copyrighted materials in history." However, these allegations have not been proven in court, and no ruling has been issued on Google's liability. The Legal Claims and Publisher Deals at the Heart of the Gemini Lawsuit The plaintiffs allege four legal claims: direct copyright infringement, contributory copyright infringement, removal or alteration of copyright-management information, and violations of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. They argue that Google obtained protected material through its book services, internet scraping, and other sources before using the content to train Gemini. Publishers provided books and journal articles to Google Books, Google Play Books, and Google Scholar under agreements that covered specific uses, such as displaying searchable excerpts, distributing ebooks, and helping users discover academic publications. The plaintiffs claim that these agreements did not authorize Google to copy entire works into datasets used for commercial generative AI development, and that Google repurposed material received through established publishing relationships for uses not covered by the contracts. The complaint also states that Google collected books and other protected material through extensive internet scraping, including sources such as pirate websites and publications behind subscription or paywalls. How This Gemini Case Differs from Google Books, and What Internal Emails Say Google previously won a copyright case related to digitizing books for search and snippet previews. In 2015, a federal appellate court ruled that these uses were transformative and protected under fair use. The plaintiffs argue that this earlier ruling covered searchable book databases and limited excerpts, not the use of entire books to train generative AI models. They claim that AI training serves a different commercial purpose and results in systems that can compete with the original works involved in training. The key difference, they say, lies between search-focused digitization and the training of generative models, which is central to their case. According to the complaint, a Google employee warned during an internal discussion that using books submitted through Google Play publishing agreements for AI development could create serious legal risks. The employee reportedly estimated that such practices could lead to fines ranging from ten to one hundred billion dollars. Other internal documents described in the complaint suggest that Google sought professionally written books to enhance the performance of its Gemini AI system. The plaintiffs claim that tests showed models trained only on public domain books performed worse than those trained on collections that included copyrighted works. The complaint states that Google aimed to include works with curated facts, organized analyses, fictional narratives, and professionally edited writing. Works Cited in the Complaint and What Gemini Is Accused of Generating The complaint highlights several works as examples. Hachette lists Peter Brown's The Wild Robot, N.K. Jemisin's The Fifth Season, Becky Lomax's Moon Glacier National Park, and Lemony Snicket's Who Could That Be at This Hour? It also mentions Turow's Innocent. Cengage includes Cognitive Psychology, Principles of Economics, Milady Standard Barbering, Nutrition: Concepts and Controversies, and Calculus: Early Transcendentals. Elsevier points to copyrighted journal articles in its section of the complaint. Turow and S.C.R.I.B.E. reference Presumed Innocent, Innocent, and Testimony. The plaintiffs claim these examples are only a sample of the books and articles allegedly copied in connection with Gemini. The filing presents examples to show that Gemini can produce material related to specific protected books. It claims the system generated content based on The Fifth Season and produced responses involving characters, events, and details from Who Could That Be at This Hour? The plaintiffs also argue Gemini can generate low-cost substitutes for professionally published works. They estimate the service could produce a 100-page murder mystery set in a quiet seaside town in approximately 20 minutes for 39 cents. The complaint states, "No publisher or author can compete with that." These time and cost figures are allegations from the plaintiffs and have not been verified by the court. Who Might Join the Class and What Remedies the Plaintiffs Are Seeking The proposed class would include owners of registered copyrights in books that have International Standard Book Numbers, as well as journal articles identified through Digital Object Identifiers or International Standard Serial Numbers. To be part of the class, members would need to show that Google copied their works from one of its services, obtained them through web scraping, or used them in connection with Gemini training. The court has not yet certified this proposed class. The plaintiffs are seeking statutory damages or compensation based on their claimed losses and Google's alleged profits, along with legal fees and other remedies available under federal copyright law. They are asking the court to stop Google from continuing what they allege to be unauthorized copying through an injunction that would restrict the use of protected books and articles in Gemini training and related AI development. The complaint also requests an accounting of the works and methods Google used to train Gemini. This includes details about the materials obtained, where they were sourced from, and how they were incorporated into Google's systems. The plaintiffs seek a court-supervised destruction of infringing copies and datasets derived from their works. It remains unclear whether such an order would be legally feasible or appropriate in this case. Publishers, authors, and academic rights holders who might be part of the proposed class should take some practical steps as the case develops. They should verify which of their titles are registered with the U.S. Copyright Office since the proposed class depends on registered works marked with ISBNs, DOIs, or ISSNs. It is also advisable to review existing agreements with Google Books, Google Play Books, and Google Scholar to understand what uses those contracts permit. Additionally, they should keep records of publication dates, distribution channels, and any communications with Google regarding the use of their works in AI training datasets. Tracking the progress of the class certification could also be important, as inclusion in any potential class will depend on the court's decision. Where the Hachette and Cengage Lawsuit Against Google Stands Now Hachette and Cengage had previously attempted to join a separate copyright lawsuit filed against Google in California in 2023, which involved authors and visual artists. Google opposed their participation, and the publishers later withdrew that effort before submitting the current case in New York. Google has not yet issued a detailed public response to the specific allegations in the New York complaint. The company will have the opportunity to respond as the case moves forward through motions, potential discovery, and class-certification processes. items.summary_html:
Hachette Book Group, Cengage Learning, Elsevier, author Scott Turow, and S.C.R.I.B.E., Inc. have filed a proposed federal class-action lawsuit against Google.

They accuse the company of copying copyrighted books and journal articles without permission to train its Gemini AI models. The lawsuit was filed on July 10, 2026. The case, Hachette Book Group Inc. et al. v. Google LLC, is under case number 1:26-cv-05870 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.

The complaint describes Google's alleged actions as "one of the most prolific infringements of copyrighted materials in history." However, these allegations have not been proven in court, and no ruling has been issued on Google's liability.

The Legal Claims and Publisher Deals at the Heart of the Gemini Lawsuit

The plaintiffs allege four legal claims: direct copyright infringement, contributory copyright infringement, removal or alteration of copyright-management information, and violations of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.

They argue that Google obtained protected material through its book services, internet scraping, and other sources before using the content to train Gemini.

Publishers provided books and journal articles to Google Books, Google Play Books, and Google Scholar under agreements that covered specific uses, such as displaying searchable excerpts, distributing ebooks, and helping users discover academic publications.

The plaintiffs claim that these agreements did not authorize Google to copy entire works into datasets used for commercial generative AI development, and that Google repurposed material received through established publishing relationships for uses not covered by the contracts.

The complaint also states that Google collected books and other protected material through extensive internet scraping, including sources such as pirate websites and publications behind subscription or paywalls.

How This Gemini Case Differs from Google Books, and What Internal Emails Say

Google previously won a copyright case related to digitizing books for search and snippet previews. In 2015, a federal appellate court ruled that these uses were transformative and protected under fair use.

The plaintiffs argue that this earlier ruling covered searchable book databases and limited excerpts, not the use of entire books to train generative AI models.

They claim that AI training serves a different commercial purpose and results in systems that can compete with the original works involved in training. The key difference, they say, lies between search-focused digitization and the training of generative models, which is central to their case.

According to the complaint, a Google employee warned during an internal discussion that using books submitted through Google Play publishing agreements for AI development could create serious legal risks. The employee reportedly estimated that such practices could lead to fines ranging from ten to one hundred billion dollars.

Other internal documents described in the complaint suggest that Google sought professionally written books to enhance the performance of its Gemini AI system.

The plaintiffs claim that tests showed models trained only on public domain books performed worse than those trained on collections that included copyrighted works. The complaint states that Google aimed to include works with curated facts, organized analyses, fictional narratives, and professionally edited writing.

Works Cited in the Complaint and What Gemini Is Accused of Generating

The complaint highlights several works as examples. Hachette lists Peter Brown's The Wild Robot, N.K. Jemisin's The Fifth Season, Becky Lomax's Moon Glacier National Park, and Lemony Snicket's Who Could That Be at This Hour?

It also mentions Turow's Innocent. Cengage includes Cognitive Psychology, Principles of Economics, Milady Standard Barbering, Nutrition: Concepts and Controversies, and Calculus: Early Transcendentals. Elsevier points to copyrighted journal articles in its section of the complaint.

Turow and S.C.R.I.B.E. reference Presumed Innocent, Innocent, and Testimony. The plaintiffs claim these examples are only a sample of the books and articles allegedly copied in connection with Gemini.

The filing presents examples to show that Gemini can produce material related to specific protected books. It claims the system generated content based on The Fifth Season and produced responses involving characters, events, and details from Who Could That Be at This Hour? The plaintiffs also argue Gemini can generate low-cost substitutes for professionally published works.

They estimate the service could produce a 100-page murder mystery set in a quiet seaside town in approximately 20 minutes for 39 cents. The complaint states, "No publisher or author can compete with that." These time and cost figures are allegations from the plaintiffs and have not been verified by the court.

Who Might Join the Class and What Remedies the Plaintiffs Are Seeking

The proposed class would include owners of registered copyrights in books that have International Standard Book Numbers, as well as journal articles identified through Digital Object Identifiers or International Standard Serial Numbers.

To be part of the class, members would need to show that Google copied their works from one of its services, obtained them through web scraping, or used them in connection with Gemini training. The court has not yet certified this proposed class.

The plaintiffs are seeking statutory damages or compensation based on their claimed losses and Google's alleged profits, along with legal fees and other remedies available under federal copyright law.

They are asking the court to stop Google from continuing what they allege to be unauthorized copying through an injunction that would restrict the use of protected books and articles in Gemini training and related AI development.

The complaint also requests an accounting of the works and methods Google used to train Gemini. This includes details about the materials obtained, where they were sourced from, and how they were incorporated into Google's systems.

The plaintiffs seek a court-supervised destruction of infringing copies and datasets derived from their works. It remains unclear whether such an order would be legally feasible or appropriate in this case.

Publishers, authors, and academic rights holders who might be part of the proposed class should take some practical steps as the case develops. They should verify which of their titles are registered with the U.S. Copyright Office since the proposed class depends on registered works marked with ISBNs, DOIs, or ISSNs.

It is also advisable to review existing agreements with Google Books, Google Play Books, and Google Scholar to understand what uses those contracts permit.

Additionally, they should keep records of publication dates, distribution channels, and any communications with Google regarding the use of their works in AI training datasets. Tracking the progress of the class certification could also be important, as inclusion in any potential class will depend on the court's decision.

Where the Hachette and Cengage Lawsuit Against Google Stands Now

Hachette and Cengage had previously attempted to join a separate copyright lawsuit filed against Google in California in 2023, which involved authors and visual artists. Google opposed their participation, and the publishers later withdrew that effort before submitting the current case in New York.

Google has not yet issued a detailed public response to the specific allegations in the New York complaint. The company will have the opportunity to respond as the case moves forward through motions, potential discovery, and class-certification processes. No trial date has been set, and the court has not ruled on any of the four claims.

Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Book Writers Sue Google Over Alleged Use of Copyrighted Books to Train Gemini appeared first on gHacks.
